title: Beginner Dev Flow
lede: Eight short cards that take you from "what is a webhook?" to a deployed LINE bot with AI, rich UI and a web app. Read them in order, or jump to the step you are on.
note: Every link, endpoint and SDK version on these cards was checked against official LINE pages or the official SDK repositories on Nov 24, 2026. The echo bots in Step 04 and the AI handler in Step 06 were run locally against signed test webhooks.

cards.title: How a LINE Bot Works
cards.summary: A LINE bot is a web server that LINE calls every time someone talks to your Official Account. Learn the four moving parts and the words you will see everywhere before you write any code.
cards.goal: Understand the round trip a message makes, from a user's phone to your server and back, and the handful of terms the LINE docs use for it.
learn: The four pieces: user, LINE Platform, your bot server, Messaging API
What a webhook event looks like
Reply messages vs push messages
Provider, channel, channel secret and channel access token

steps.title: A user sends a message
steps.body: Someone opens the chat with your LINE Official Account (OA) and types "Hello", taps a button, or adds you as a friend.

steps.title: LINE calls your webhook
steps.body: The LINE Platform sends an HTTPS POST to the webhook URL you registered. The JSON body holds a list of `events` (message, follow, unfollow, postback and more), and the `x-line-signature` header proves it came from LINE.

steps.title: Your server checks and reads it
steps.body: Your bot verifies the signature with the channel secret, then looks at each event: who sent it (`source.userId`), what they sent, and the one-time `replyToken`.

steps.title: Your server answers through the Messaging API
steps.body: You call `https://api.line.me` with your channel access token. Most bots use the Reply API with the `replyToken`. To message someone later, without a fresh event, you use the Push API.

steps.title: LINE delivers the message
steps.body: The user sees your answer in the chat. A single reply or push request can carry up to five message objects.

terms: The company or person that owns your channels. Users get a different user ID for each provider.
The connection between your app and the LINE Platform. A bot uses a Messaging API channel.
The key used to check webhook signatures. Keep it on the server.
The bearer token your server sends when it calls the Messaging API.
Your server's HTTPS endpoint. Only one can be set per channel.
A one-time token inside an event, used to answer that event with the Reply API.

code.label: A simplified webhook body for one text message (shape taken from the LINE docs)

gotchas.title: One webhook URL per channel
gotchas.body: A channel can point at only one bot server. If two tools both need the messages (say, a CRM and your own bot), one of them has to forward to the other.

gotchas.title: Provider choice decides user IDs
gotchas.body: The same person has a different user ID under each provider, and a channel cannot move to another provider later. Put your bot, LINE Login and LIFF channels under one provider you control.

gotchas.title: Don't filter by IP address
gotchas.body: LINE does not publish the IP addresses that send webhooks. Check the signature instead of using an IP allowlist.

gotchas.title: The same event can arrive twice
gotchas.body: Network problems and redelivery can send an event more than once. Use `webhookEventId` to skip events you already handled.

cards.title: Account, Official Account & Messaging API Setup
cards.summary: Every bot starts as a LINE Official Account with the Messaging API turned on. Create the account, enable the API, and collect the two secrets your code needs.
cards.goal: Finish with a working Messaging API channel, a channel secret and a channel access token saved in a local `.env` file, and auto-replies turned off so they don't fight your bot.
learn: Why you now start in LINE Official Account Manager, not the Developers Console
Where to find the channel secret and channel access token
Which token type to use
Why to turn off the default auto-reply

steps.title: Create a LINE Official Account
steps.body: Register a Business ID (with your LINE account or an email address) and fill in the entry form. Your new account appears in LINE Official Account Manager at manager.line.biz.

steps.title: Enable the Messaging API
steps.body: In LINE Official Account Manager, open Settings, then Messaging API, and enable it. The first time, you register as a developer (name and email) and choose a provider. The provider cannot be changed later, so pick one you control.

steps.title: Open the channel in the LINE Developers Console
steps.body: Log in to developers.line.biz/console with the same account, open the provider, and you will see the new Messaging API channel.

steps.title: Copy the channel secret
steps.body: On the channel's Basic settings tab, copy the Channel secret. You need the Admin role on the channel to see or reissue it.

steps.title: Issue a channel access token
steps.body: On the Messaging API tab, issue a channel access token for testing. For production, LINE recommends a channel access token with a user-specified expiration (v2.1); see the table below.

steps.title: Turn off auto-replies
steps.body: Greeting messages and Auto-reply messages are on by default. While you build, turn them off in LINE Official Account Manager so you can tell which answers come from your bot.

steps.title: Add your OA as a friend
steps.body: Scan the QR code on the Messaging API tab with your phone. You will test every step from this chat.

table.caption: Channel access token types (from the LINE Developers "Channel access token" page, checked Nov 24, 2026)
head: Type
Validity
Tokens per channel

code.label: .env in your project folder (never commit this file)
code.code:
CHANNEL_SECRET=<channel secret from the Basic settings tab>
CHANNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN=<token from the Messaging API tab>

gotchas.title: Looking for "Create channel" in the console
gotchas.body: Since September 4, 2024 you can no longer create a Messaging API channel directly in the LINE Developers Console. Start from LINE Official Account Manager.

gotchas.title: Leaving auto-reply on
gotchas.body: With the default Auto-reply messages enabled, users get the canned answer and your bot's answer, and you can't tell which is which. Turn it off while you build.

gotchas.title: Mixing up secret and token
gotchas.body: The channel secret checks incoming webhooks; the channel access token authorizes outgoing API calls. Swapping them makes signature checks fail or API calls return 401.

gotchas.title: Picking a provider in a hurry
gotchas.body: A channel can't move to another provider, and user IDs differ per provider. Don't create your bot under an agency's or a tool vendor's provider unless you mean to.

cards.title: Local Dev Environment & HTTPS Webhook Tunnel
cards.summary: LINE can only call a public HTTPS address, not your laptop. Set up Node.js or Python, then use a tunnel so LINE can reach the bot running on your machine.
cards.goal: Run a bot on `localhost:3000`, expose it through a temporary HTTPS tunnel, and see the Verify button in the console say Success.
learn: The runtime versions the current official SDKs need
How to start a project for Node.js or Python
Two free ways to get a temporary HTTPS URL
How to register and verify the webhook URL

steps.title: Install a runtime
steps.body: The Node.js SDK `@line/bot-sdk` 11.4.0 needs Node.js 22 or newer. The Python SDK `line-bot-sdk` 3.27.0 needs Python 3.10 or newer. (Latest versions as of Nov 24, 2026.)

steps.title: Create the project
steps.body: Make a folder, install the SDK and a web framework (Express for Node.js, Flask for Python), and put your two secrets in `.env` as in Step 02.

steps.title: Start your bot locally
steps.body: Use the echo bot from Step 04. It listens on port 3000 with the webhook path `/callback`.

steps.title: Open a tunnel
steps.body: Run `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000` (no account needed; prints a temporary trycloudflare.com URL) or `ngrok http 3000` (needs a free ngrok account and authtoken).

steps.title: Register the webhook URL
steps.body: In the Developers Console, Messaging API tab, edit Webhook URL to `https://<your-tunnel-host>/callback`, click Update, then Verify. Turn on Use webhook.

steps.title: Send a test message
steps.body: Message your OA from your phone and watch your terminal log the event.

code.label: Node.js project
code.code:
mkdir my-line-bot && cd my-line-bot
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install @line/bot-sdk express
# Node.js 22 can load .env without extra packages:
node --env-file=.env index.js

code.label: Python project
code.code:
mkdir my-line-bot && cd my-line-bot
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install line-bot-sdk flask
export $(grep -v '^#' .env | xargs)   # load .env into this shell
python app.py

code.label: Temporary HTTPS tunnel (pick one, in a second terminal)
code.code:
cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000
# or
ngrok http 3000

gotchas.title: Using http:// or a self-signed certificate
gotchas.body: The webhook URL must be HTTPS with a certificate from a widely trusted authority. `http://localhost` and self-signed certificates are rejected.

gotchas.title: Forgetting the path
gotchas.body: Register `https://.../callback`, not just the host. Without the path your server answers 404 and Verify fails.

gotchas.title: Tunnel URL changed
gotchas.body: A cloudflared Quick Tunnel URL stops working when you stop the process, and a new run gives a new URL. Update the webhook URL each time, or use a fixed domain later.

gotchas.title: Verify sends no events
gotchas.body: The Verify button posts a body with an empty `events` array. Your code must accept that and still answer 200.

cards.title: Signature Verification & Your First Echo Bot
cards.summary: Your first bot repeats whatever the user types. It also teaches the two habits every LINE bot needs: check the signature on the raw body, and answer with the reply token right away.
cards.goal: Get a working echo bot in Node.js or Python that rejects fake requests and replies to real ones.
learn: How `x-line-signature` is checked
The minimal echo bot with the current official SDKs
Why the raw body matters
Reply token rules

steps.title: Keep the raw body
steps.body: Read the request body exactly as it arrived. Don't parse, pretty-print or re-encode it before the signature check.

steps.title: Check the signature
steps.body: Compute HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with your channel secret, base64-encode it, and compare it with `x-line-signature`. The SDKs do this for you: `line.middleware()` in Node.js and `WebhookHandler.handle()` in Python.

steps.title: Reject anything that fails
steps.body: If the header is missing or doesn't match, stop and return an error. Don't process the events.

steps.title: Reply to text messages
steps.body: For each `message` event with a text message, call the Reply API with the event's `replyToken` and up to five message objects.

steps.title: Return 200
steps.body: Answer the webhook with HTTP 200 so LINE knows you received it.

code.label: Node.js: index.js (@line/bot-sdk 11.x, Express 5). Tested locally: valid signature 200, bad signature 401.
Python: app.py (line-bot-sdk 3.x, Flask). Tested locally: valid signature 200, bad signature 400.
Check a signature by hand with openssl (example values from the LINE docs)

gotchas.title: Parsing JSON before the check
gotchas.body: In Express, a global `app.use(express.json())` placed before `line.middleware()` consumes the body, and every request fails the signature check. We reproduced this: even correctly signed requests got 401. Mount `line.middleware()` on the webhook route only, with no JSON parser in front.

gotchas.title: Reusing or delaying the reply token
gotchas.body: A reply token works once. The reference says to use it within one minute of receiving the webhook and warns the limit can change, so reply as soon as you can. A second reply with the same token fails with "Invalid reply token".

gotchas.title: One reply per event
gotchas.body: Need to send three bubbles? Put them in one reply request (up to five message objects) instead of making three calls.

gotchas.title: Secret was reissued
gotchas.body: If signatures suddenly fail after working fine, someone with Admin rights may have reissued the channel secret. Copy the new one from Basic settings.

links.label: Official Python SDK with Flask synopsis

cards.title: Interactive UI: Quick Replies, Flex Messages & Rich Menus
cards.summary: Buttons beat typing. Use quick replies for the next choice, Flex Messages for card layouts, and a rich menu for the menu that stays at the bottom of the chat.
cards.goal: Know which of the three UI tools fits a job, and send your first quick reply and Flex Message.
learn: Quick reply buttons and postback actions
Flex Message structure and the Flex Message Simulator
The new 20-level box nesting limit
Two ways to build a rich menu

steps.title: Quick replies for the next step
steps.body: Attach up to 13 buttons to any message. They show above the keyboard and suit short choices like "Yes / No" or "Pick a branch".

steps.title: Postbacks for hidden data
steps.body: A postback action sends a `postback` event with your `data` string to the webhook, so you can tell which button was tapped without parsing text.

steps.title: Flex Messages for rich cards
steps.body: Flex Messages are JSON layouts built from bubbles, boxes, text, images and buttons. Design them in the Flex Message Simulator, then paste the JSON into your code.

steps.title: Mind the nesting limit
steps.body: Since November 19, 2026, a Flex Message whose boxes nest deeper than 20 levels (the outermost box is level 1) is rejected with 400 Bad Request. Check depth if your layouts are generated by code or an LLM.

steps.title: Rich menus for always-on navigation
steps.body: A rich menu is the image menu at the bottom of the chat. Build a default menu in LINE Official Account Manager (quick, with click statistics), or use the API for per-user menus and tab switching.

code.label: Quick reply with a message action, a postback action and a location action
Smallest Flex Message (from the LINE docs). Put it in the messages array of a reply.
Default rich menu with the API: create, upload image, set default
code.code:
# 1. Create the rich menu (returns a richMenuId)
curl -X POST https://api.line.me/v2/bot/richmenu \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CHANNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @richmenu.json

# 2. Upload the image (note the api-data.line.me host)
curl -X POST https://api-data.line.me/v2/bot/richmenu/{richMenuId}/content \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CHANNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: image/png" \
  -T richmenu.png

# 3. Make it the default menu for everyone
curl -X POST https://api.line.me/v2/bot/user/all/richmenu/{richMenuId} \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CHANNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN"

gotchas.title: Flex boxes nested too deep
gotchas.body: Recursive templates and LLM-generated layouts can exceed 20 levels of boxes and now fail with 400. Flatten the layout or cap the depth.

gotchas.title: Missing altText
gotchas.body: Every Flex Message needs `altText`. It is what users see in notifications and the chat list.

gotchas.title: Testing quick replies on desktop
gotchas.body: Quick reply is supported on LINE for iOS and Android. Test it on a phone.

gotchas.title: Editing a rich menu from the wrong tool
gotchas.body: A rich menu made in LINE Official Account Manager can only be edited there, and one made with the API can only be edited by the API. Pick one tool per menu.

cards.title: Connecting an AI / LLM (or No-Code Builders)
cards.summary: An AI bot is the echo bot with a model call in the middle. The hard part is time: show a loading animation, keep short per-user memory, and reply before the token goes stale.
cards.goal: Wire a language model into your bot without timeouts or double replies, or pick a no-code builder if you'd rather not run a server.
learn: Acknowledge the webhook first, then think
The official loading animation endpoint
Simple per-user memory keyed by `userId`
No-code and low-code paths: Dify, n8n, Botpress, LINE Bot MCP Server

steps.title: Acknowledge fast, work after
steps.body: LINE recommends processing webhook events asynchronously. Return 200 first, then call the model, so slow answers don't hold up the next webhook.

steps.title: Show the loading animation
steps.body: Call `POST https://api.line.me/v2/bot/chat/loading/start` with `chatId` (the user ID) and `loadingSeconds` (5 to 60). It works in one-on-one chats only, shows only while the user has the chat open, and disappears when your message arrives.

steps.title: Remember a little context
steps.body: Store the last few turns per `source.userId`. An in-memory Map is fine on your laptop; use Redis or a database once you deploy, because servers restart.

steps.title: Reply once, quickly
steps.body: Use the reply token as soon as the answer is ready. If the model is too slow and the token has expired, a push message still works, but push counts against your monthly message quota.

steps.title: Or skip the server
steps.body: Dify: the LINE Connect plugin (community-built, listed on Dify Marketplace) links a Dify app to an OA. n8n: use the Webhook node to receive events and the HTTP Request node to call the Messaging API. Botpress has a LINE integration. LY also publishes LINE Bot MCP Server (a preview) so an AI agent can send messages through MCP tools.

code.label: Node.js: AI handler with loading animation and per-user memory (@line/bot-sdk 11.x)
The loading animation endpoint with curl (from the LINE docs)

gotchas.title: Waiting for the model inside the webhook
gotchas.body: If you call the model before answering the webhook, slow responses pile up. Acknowledge first. On serverless hosts, work after the response may be cut off, so use the platform's background task feature or a queue.

gotchas.title: Loading animation in a group
gotchas.body: The animation only works for one-on-one chats. Passing a group ID won't show anything.

gotchas.title: Using n8n's built-in Line node
gotchas.body: That node was for LINE Notify, which ended on April 1, 2025, and n8n marks it deprecated from version 1.64.0. It cannot run a Messaging API bot; use Webhook plus HTTP Request nodes.

gotchas.title: Assuming replies are always free
gotchas.body: LINE for Business Thailand announced that from February 1, 2027 the Reply API is free only for the first 25,000 messages a month. Plan costs for AI bots in Thailand with that in mind (details in Step 08).

cards.title: Beyond Chat: LIFF & LINE MINI Apps
cards.summary: Some jobs need a real screen: forms, bookings, carts. LIFF and LINE MINI Apps open your web app inside LINE and tell it who the user is, with no separate app install.
cards.goal: Know when to move from chat to a web app, which channel type to use, and how to scaffold your first LIFF app.
learn: What LIFF and LINE MINI App are
Why new LIFF apps belong on a LINE Login or LINE MINI App channel
Scaffolding with Create LIFF App or LIFF CLI
Verified vs unverified MINI Apps

steps.title: Decide if chat is enough
steps.body: If users must fill several fields, pick dates or browse a list, a web page is kinder than ten chat turns. Open it from a rich menu, a Flex button or a link.

steps.title: Pick the channel type
steps.body: LIFF apps can only be added to LINE Login or LINE MINI App channels, not to Messaging API channels. LINE recommends creating new LIFF apps as LINE MINI Apps, because LIFF will be folded into the LINE MINI App brand. Keep the channel under the same provider as your bot so user IDs match.

steps.title: Scaffold the app
steps.body: Run `npx @line/create-liff-app` and choose a template (vanilla, React, Vue, Svelte, Next.js or Nuxt). Or install LIFF CLI (`@line/liff-cli`) to add channels, create LIFF apps and run `liff-cli init` from the terminal.

steps.title: Initialize LIFF on every page load
steps.body: Call `liff.init()` before any other LIFF method, then read the user's profile or send messages on their behalf.

steps.title: Grow into a MINI App
steps.body: A new LINE MINI App starts unverified, with some features restricted, until it passes LINE's verification review. Since March 11, 2026, anyone can publish LINE MINI Apps in Taiwan and Thailand.

code.label: Scaffold a LIFF app (official tools)
code.code:
npx @line/create-liff-app
# or, with LIFF CLI
npm install @line/liff-cli
npx liff-cli channel add <channelId>   # prompts for the channel secret
npx liff-cli init --channel-id <channelId> --name my-app \
  --endpoint-url https://example.com --view-type full

code.label: Minimal LIFF page script

gotchas.title: Adding LIFF to the bot's Messaging API channel
gotchas.body: That is no longer allowed for new LIFF apps. Create a LINE Login or LINE MINI App channel under the same provider.

gotchas.title: Different provider, different user ID
gotchas.body: If the LIFF channel and the bot sit under different providers, the same person shows two different user IDs and you can't join the data.

gotchas.title: Calling LIFF methods before init
gotchas.body: Run `liff.init()` on every page load and wait for it to finish before calling other methods or changing the URL's query parameters.

cards.title: Deploying, Quotas & Production Checklist
cards.summary: Move the bot from your laptop to a real HTTPS host, keep tokens out of Git, and know which messages cost money. Thailand's Reply API rules change on February 1, 2027.
cards.goal: Ship a bot you can leave running: hosted on HTTPS, secrets safe, costs understood, and logs you can debug with.
learn: What counts toward your monthly message quota
Where to read official prices for Thailand, Japan and Taiwan
The 2027 Reply API change in Thailand
A short production checklist

steps.title: Host it on HTTPS
steps.body: Any host with a trusted certificate works: a small VPS, a container platform or a serverless function. Point the webhook URL at it, click Verify, and keep the same `/callback` path.

steps.title: Move secrets to the host
steps.body: Set `CHANNEL_SECRET` and `CHANNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN` in the host's environment or secret manager. For long-running bots, LINE recommends channel access tokens with a user-specified expiration (v2.1) or stateless tokens over the long-lived token.

steps.title: Know what is counted
steps.body: On the LINE Developers pricing page, push, multicast, broadcast and narrowcast messages count toward your plan; reply messages do not. Messages are counted per recipient, not per message object. When you run out, sends fail with an error instead of going through.

steps.title: Check the official plan for your country
steps.body: Plans differ by country. As an example, the LINE Developers pricing page lists Japan's plans as Communication (free, up to 200 messages a month), Light (JPY 5,000, up to 5,000) and Standard (JPY 15,000, up to 30,000), excluding tax (checked Nov 24, 2026). For Thailand and Taiwan, read the local LINE for Business pages linked below.

steps.title: Plan for Thailand's Reply API change
steps.body: LINE for Business Thailand (announced Nov 9, 2026): from February 1, 2027, the Reply API stays free for the first 25,000 messages a month; above that you need the 5,000 THB a month Unlimited package, and to keep using the Reply API you register through an Agency Partner to move the account into AGP. Auto-response set up in LINE Official Account Manager is not affected.

steps.title: Log and handle retries
steps.body: Log the `x-line-request-id` response header, time, endpoint and status for API calls, as the development guidelines suggest. If you turn on webhook redelivery, skip duplicates by `webhookEventId`.

checklist: `.env` is in `.gitignore` and no token appears in Git history
Signature check runs on the raw body and rejects bad requests
Webhook returns 200 quickly; slow work runs after
Auto-reply in LINE Official Account Manager is off (or set on purpose)
You know how to revoke a channel access token and reissue the channel secret yourself
Third-party tools holding your token are on your list, so you can rotate it if they are breached
No load tests or bulk test traffic against the LINE Platform

code.label: Check this month's quota and usage
code.code:
# Monthly limit for counted messages
curl -s https://api.line.me/v2/bot/message/quota \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CHANNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN"

# Counted messages sent so far this month
curl -s https://api.line.me/v2/bot/message/quota/consumption \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CHANNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN"

gotchas.title: Committing .env
gotchas.body: A pushed token is a leaked token, even if you delete it in the next commit. Revoke it and issue a new one, then reissue the channel secret if that leaked too.

gotchas.title: Tokens held by outside tools
gotchas.body: In November 2026, Dentsu Digital reported that a breach of its TONARIWA tool exposed LINE OA integration access tokens for client companies. If a vendor holds your token, know how to revoke and reissue it yourself.

gotchas.title: Push fallback eats the quota
gotchas.body: Falling back to push when a reply token expires is fine, but every push counts. A slow AI bot that always pushes can hit the free limit fast.

gotchas.title: Load testing through LINE
gotchas.body: The development guidelines prohibit load tests and mass requests through the LINE Platform. Load-test your own server with fake signed webhooks instead.
